strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: useful conformal prediction sets for extremely long-tailed, many-class classification.

Introduces two clear contributions: prevalence-adjusted softmax, motivated by an oracle optimization of macro-coverage versus expected set size, and FUZZY CP, which interpolates between standard and classwise calibration while retaining marginal coverage through reconformalization.

The theoretical development is generally well motivated, with an explicit Neyman–Pearson characterization, finite-sample marginal validity for FUZZY CP, and endpoint analysis connecting Raw FUZZY to standard and classwise conformal prediction.

Evaluation uses two genuinely large, long-tailed biodiversity datasets with 1,081 and 8,142 classes and compares against relevant standard, classwise, exact-classwise, and clustered conformal baselines.

The results consistently illustrate the central practical trade-off: the proposed methods substantially improve rare-class or macro-coverage without incurring the enormous sets produced by classwise conformal prediction. The endangered-species case study is particularly compelling.

The paper is clearly written, candid about the lack of a guarantee for INTERP-Q, and includes useful analyses of alternative mappings, parameter behavior, weighted macro-coverage, and simulated downstream decision-making.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol violates the exchangeability condition underlying the advertised coverage guarantees: the same validation data are used both to select the model checkpoint and to calibrate conformal thresholds. Showing that one standard-CP threshold is numerically close when computed on validation and test data does not establish validity, particularly for PAS and FUZZY CP. A clean model-selection/calibration split or repeated experiment is needed.

The main empirical evidence consists of dense Pareto plots without numerical tables, uncertainty intervals, or repetitions over data splits and random seeds. This makes it difficult to assess the magnitude and stability of improvements, especially for rare-class metrics with high sampling variance.

Evaluation is limited to two closely related biodiversity image datasets, one backbone, and one training recipe. Broader evidence across long-tailed domains, architectures, and classifier-quality or calibration regimes is needed to support the general claims.

Several design choices lack proper validation, including the fixed 5,000-example reconformalization split, bandwidth rescaling, bandwidth grid, and parameter-selection procedure. The paper suggests tuning to a desired set size on calibration data but does not evaluate the resulting end-to-end selection procedure on independent data.

The human-decision analysis uses only idealized expert and uniform-random guesser models. It does not provide behavioral evidence that the improved coverage–size trade-offs translate into better real human decisions or lower effort.

The reproducibility statement says that code is available but provides no repository or supplementary pointer in the manuscript, and important implementation details such as seeds, preprocessing, augmentation, optimizer, batch size, and checkpoint-selection rule are missing.

The formal conditions of the Raw FUZZY endpoint result appear weaker than what its proof uses: the proof requires ratios such as h_sigma(u,v)/h_sigma(u,u) to converge to zero or one, whereas the proposition states only absolute convergence conditions. This is satisfied by the Gaussian kernel used experimentally but should be corrected in the theorem.

There are smaller technical and presentation issues: the claim that prevalence normalization plus noise keeps mappings in [0,1] is false near the endpoints, the proof discussion momentarily reverses the small- and large-bandwidth limits, and the main result figure is excessively crowded.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: useful conformal prediction sets under extreme class imbalance and thousands of labels.
The PAS score has a clean likelihood-ratio motivation, and the Neyman–Pearson derivation clearly characterizes the oracle trade-off between expected set size and macro-coverage.
The label-weighted formulation provides a useful common perspective on standard, classwise, and fuzzy conformal prediction.
Experiments cover two genuinely long-tailed datasets, include truncated variants for more reliable classwise evaluation, and compare several established conformal baselines.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol knowingly reuses the validation data for checkpoint selection and conformal calibration, violating the exchangeability assumption underlying the advertised guarantees. Showing that one standard-CP threshold is similar on validation and test data for one dataset does not establish validity, especially for class-dependent procedures.

The FUZZY reconformalization guarantee is not specified consistently. The text describes tilde-alpha as a miscoverage parameter, Equation 16 defines it as a quantile of transformed scores, and Proposition 3 then says to run Raw FUZZY at “level tilde-alpha.” The required complement and boundary/tie conventions are unclear, so the proposition does not unambiguously establish coverage for the stated algorithm.

The oracle optimality of PAS assumes the true conditional and label distributions. No approximation or robustness result connects this oracle statement to estimated, potentially miscalibrated neural-network probabilities and empirical prevalences. Marginal conformal validity alone does not support the stronger empirical claims about macro-coverage.

Macro-coverage and other classwise metrics on the original long-tailed test sets can be extremely noisy because rare classes have very few test examples. The paper provides no confidence intervals, repeated splits, seed variation, or statistical tests, yet makes strong Pareto-frontier and consistency claims from dense plots.

The evaluation lacks important alternatives that could explain the gains, including established prior correction or logit adjustment, class-balanced calibration, shrinkage or hierarchical pooling of classwise quantiles, taxonomy-based grouping, and simple top-k or size-controlled predictors.

The main quantitative figure is overcrowded and supplies few readily auditable numbers. Numerical tables, uncertainty estimates, and per-dataset calibration sample counts are needed to substantiate claims such as PAS setting the Pareto frontier.

The human-decision experiment uses only analytically constructed expert-versus-uniform-guesser models. These extremes provide little evidence about actual human utility, search effort, or behavior in the motivating plant-identification application.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the code statement contains no link, and key training details such as optimizer, batch size, augmentation, random seeds, and complete checkpoint-selection procedure are missing.

INTERP-Q explicitly lacks a coverage guarantee, while FUZZY relies on a heuristic prevalence embedding, injected random noise, and a broad bandwidth sweep. The paper does not provide a principled, independently validated parameter-selection evaluation.

Overall, the ideas are promising, but the guarantee ambiguity, invalid calibration protocol, missing uncertainty analysis, and incomplete baseline coverage leave the central empirical and validity claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: producing useful conformal prediction sets for genuinely long-tailed, many-class classification, where standard marginal and classwise methods exhibit severe practical limitations.

The PAS score has a clean decision-theoretic motivation. The Neyman–Pearson derivation characterizes oracle sets that optimally trade expected set size against macro-coverage and extends naturally to application-specific weighted macro-coverage.

FUZZY CP offers a conceptually appealing interpolation between marginal and classwise calibration, while the reconformalization idea aims to retain finite-sample marginal validity. INTERP-Q is also a useful, simple empirical baseline despite lacking a guarantee.

The experiments cover two realistic biodiversity datasets with up to 8,142 classes, compare against relevant conformal baselines, report several complementary coverage metrics, and include truncated datasets that permit more reliable classwise evaluation. The observed size–coverage improvements are substantial and generally consistent.
The paper is clearly motivated and organized, and the plant-identification case study effectively illustrates why rare-class coverage and manageable set size matter simultaneously.
weaknesses: The empirical protocol reuses the validation/calibration data to select the classifier checkpoint. The paper explicitly acknowledges that this violates the exchangeability condition underlying the advertised conformal guarantees, but checking that one Standard-CP quantile is numerically similar on validation and test data does not validate the guarantees for PAS or FUZZY. A clean training/model-selection/calibration split is needed.

Proposition 3 is justified only by a one-line appeal to exchangeability. The manuscript does not establish carefully that running Raw FUZZY at the recalibrated level is exactly equivalent to thresholding the proposed discrete score. In particular, the score uses a strict inequality in its empirical CDF, whereas split conformal includes scores at or below its quantile; ties have positive probability because this score takes finitely many rank-like values. The claimed finite-sample guarantee therefore needs a rigorous tie-aware proof or randomized correction.

The evidence is largely based on one architecture and apparently one training run/split per dataset. There are no uncertainty intervals, repeated runs, or numerical result tables, while the principal trade-off figure is very dense. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness and exact magnitude of the gains, especially for metrics aggregated over rare classes.

The truncated-dataset construction creates a class-balanced test set but a differently distributed calibration set, after which marginal quantities are reweighted using training prevalences. The paper should state precisely which target distribution the guarantee concerns and justify why its calibration procedure is valid for that reweighted distribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the stated code URL is blank, and important training and evaluation details such as optimizer, batch size, augmentation, random seeds, checkpoint-selection procedure, and baseline tuning are omitted.

PAS is elegant but closely resembles prior/prevalence adjustment, and FUZZY's chosen prevalence mapping and bandwidth scaling are heuristic. Evaluation across additional domains, classifier families, and stronger prevalence-adjusted or long-tail calibration baselines would better establish the generality and novelty of the contribution.

The simulated human study uses only expert-verifier/random-guesser mixtures and supplies no behavioral validation. It is an illustrative analysis rather than evidence that the proposed sets improve real human-AI decisions.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: producing useful conformal prediction sets for large, severely long-tailed label spaces.

PAS is simple and well motivated by an oracle characterization showing that thresholding prevalence-adjusted posterior probabilities optimally trades expected set size against weighted macro-coverage.
INTERP-Q provides an intuitive, tunable continuum between standard and classwise conformal prediction, with a valid—albeit conservative—marginal coverage lower bound.
Experiments use two challenging real-world datasets with 1,081 and 8,142 classes and compare against relevant standard, classwise, and clustered conformal baselines.

The empirical improvements are practically meaningful: for example, on Pl@ntNet-300K at roughly 90% marginal coverage, PAS reduces the fraction of classes below 50% coverage from 0.389 to 0.167 while increasing average set size only from 1.57 to 2.57.
The appendices provide proofs, truncated-dataset evaluations, alternative scores and mappings, focal-loss experiments, and a useful application-focused case study.
weaknesses: The practical methods do not directly guarantee the paper's main desideratum. PAS guarantees only marginal coverage, not macro- or class-conditional coverage, while INTERP-Q guarantees only 1-2α marginal coverage rather than the nominal 1-α level.

The novelty is meaningful but relatively incremental: PAS is standard conformal prediction with a prior-adjusted score, and INTERP-Q is a simple interpolation of two existing thresholds. The main theoretical results largely establish oracle ranking and basic coverage properties rather than a deeper characterization of finite-sample classwise performance.

The empirical scope is limited to two closely related biodiversity image-classification datasets and one architecture. Evidence from other long-tailed domains, such as medical diagnosis or text classification, would strengthen the generality claim.

Reported class-conditional metrics lack uncertainty intervals or repetitions across data splits and training seeds. This is particularly concerning for rare classes, where empirical coverage estimates are noisy; truncated-dataset experiments help but do not fully address variability of the headline results.

Choosing τ to meet a desired set size on the calibration data is explicitly acknowledged to violate exchangeability, but the paper neither supplies a validity-preserving tuning procedure nor quantifies the resulting coverage risk.

The simulated-human evaluation uses idealized expert/random-guesser mixtures and therefore provides limited evidence for actual human utility; no user study or empirically validated behavioral model is included.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: optimizer, batch size, augmentation, seeds, and several implementation choices are omitted, and the manuscript's code-availability statement does not provide an accessible link.

Some claims are overstated, particularly that PAS is 'Pareto optimal': the formal result requires oracle probabilities, whereas the implemented method uses imperfect estimated probabilities and is only empirically nondominated among the tested methods.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant failure mode of conformal prediction in long-tailed, many-class problems: marginally valid sets can systematically neglect rare classes, while classwise calibration can produce unusably large sets.

The prevalence-adjusted softmax score is simple, computationally inexpensive, and motivated by a clean oracle result showing that thresholding p(y|x)/p(y) optimally trades expected set size against macro-coverage under known distributions.

The experiments use two genuinely large, long-tailed datasets with 1,081 and 8,142 classes and compare against standard, classwise, and clustered conformal baselines across several coverage and efficiency metrics.

The empirical improvements are practically meaningful on Pl@ntNet-300K: PAS substantially improves macro-coverage and the fraction of poorly covered classes while increasing average set size only modestly.

The appendices contain proofs, dataset construction details, additional baselines, truncated-dataset evaluations, focal-loss experiments, and weighted coverage experiments targeting endangered species.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. PAS is essentially a prevalence-adjusted likelihood-ratio score derived through a standard Neyman-Pearson argument, while INTERP-Q is a direct linear interpolation of two existing conformal thresholds. Much of the theoretical development formalizes relatively elementary observations.

INTERP-Q has only a 1−2α marginal-coverage guarantee, which is substantially weaker than the nominal 1−α guarantee expected from conformal prediction. More seriously, the recommended practical procedure selects the interpolation parameter using the same calibration set; the paper explicitly acknowledges that this violates exchangeability but provides neither a valid selection procedure nor an empirical stress test of the resulting coverage.

The strongest claims are overstated. Describing PAS as empirically “Pareto optimal” is justified only relative to a small collection of evaluated methods, and its oracle optimality depends on accurate estimates of p(y|x) and p(y). The paper provides no approximation, robustness, or consistency result connecting the learned PAS score to the oracle solution.

The evaluation reports results from apparently one training and data split, without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates. This is particularly problematic because the main class-conditional metrics are extremely noisy for rare classes—the exact regime on which the conclusions depend.

The empirical scope is narrower than it first appears: both primary datasets are fine-grained biodiversity image datasets, both use the same ResNet-50 pipeline, and the focal-loss experiment is only a minor variation. Evidence from another modality or substantially different long-tailed application is absent.

The simulated-human evaluation is based only on two extreme toy behaviors—perfect verification and uniform guessing—and mixtures of them. It provides little evidence for claims about actual human utility, search effort, or real decision-making with large candidate sets.

The paper does not provide a principled way to choose the central trade-off parameters τ or λ before observing test performance. Most results trace entire trade-off curves, which demonstrates attainable behavior but does not establish the performance of a deployable, pre-specified procedure.

The weighted endangered-species study averages over only 33 at-risk classes and provides no uncertainty analysis. Consequently, claims of improved conservation utility and no adverse effect on other classes are not strongly supported.

Overall, the work is technically plausible and contains useful empirical observations, but the contributions and evidence fall slightly short of the standard for acceptance at a top-tier venue: a validity-preserving tuning method, repeated-split uncertainty analysis, broader evaluation, and more careful qualification of the optimality and practical-utility claims are needed.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: useful conformal prediction for extremely long-tailed, many-class classification, where standard marginal and classwise methods exhibit a severe coverage–set-size trade-off.

The prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS) score has a clean decision-theoretic motivation. The Neyman–Pearson analysis clearly characterizes oracle sets that optimize expected size versus weighted macro-coverage.

INTERP-Q is simple, computationally practical, and provides a useful tunable continuum between standard and classwise conformal prediction. Its 1−2α marginal-coverage guarantee is valid, albeit conservative.
The evaluation is unusually well matched to the motivating setting, using two genuinely large, long-tailed datasets with 1,081 and 8,142 classes, rather than small balanced benchmarks.

Experiments compare against relevant standard, classwise, and clustered conformal baselines and evaluate several complementary quantities, including macro-coverage, undercoverage, marginal coverage, and set size.

The empirical improvements are practically meaningful. For example, on Pl@ntNet-300K at α=0.1, PAS reduces the fraction of classes below 50% coverage from 0.389 to 0.167 while increasing average set size only from 1.57 to 2.57.

The appendices provide proofs, detailed dataset construction, additional baselines, focal-loss experiments, truncated datasets with more reliable classwise evaluation, endangered-species weighting, and simulated decision-maker analyses.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually polished, with a compelling real-world case study and an appropriate discussion of broader impacts.
weaknesses: PAS is oracle-optimal only when the true conditional and class prevalence are known. With estimated probabilities, it retains marginal conformal validity but has no finite-sample macro-coverage or near-optimality guarantee; the practical success therefore depends on classifier quality and prevalence estimation.
INTERP-Q guarantees only 1−2α coverage, weaker than the nominal 1−α guarantee of the alternatives. Its near-nominal empirical coverage is encouraging but not theoretically ensured.

Choosing the interpolation parameter τ remains unresolved. The paper sweeps τ using test performance, while its suggested calibration-set selection is acknowledged to violate exchangeability; a coverage-preserving parameter-selection procedure would materially strengthen the method.

The claim that PAS is “Pareto optimal” should be qualified as empirical Pareto optimality among the evaluated configurations. The oracle proposition does not establish Pareto optimality of the estimated PAS procedure.

Results use only biodiversity image datasets and essentially one model family. Additional domains, architectures, and stronger long-tail training or calibration approaches would better establish generality.

Class-conditional estimates on the original long-tailed test sets can be highly noisy, and the paper reports no uncertainty intervals or repeated-split variability. The truncated-dataset experiments help, but they also remove the most extreme tail classes.
The simulated human models are stylized extremes or mixtures thereof and do not substitute for a user study, so conclusions about downstream human decision utility should remain cautious.

There are minor presentation inconsistencies: the prose attributes average set sizes 7.6 and 55.8 to τ=0.99, whereas Tables 3–4 associate them with τ=0.999, and the opening of one Proposition 7 proof reverses the stated small-/large-bandwidth limits before the subsequent derivation uses the correct direction.
